items.title: Netcompany Ineos sign US rider Riley Sheehan as seventh new arrival for 2027
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Netcompany Ineos have continued their rebuild for the 2027 season with the announcement of their seventh new signing, US rider Riley Sheehan, who joins from NSN on a two-year deal.

Sheehan, 26, has three professional victories to his name, from Paris-Tours in 2023, and at the Circuit de Wallonie and a stage of the Czech Tour from this past season. He will bolster the British team as a versatile Classics rider.

"Joining Netcompany Ineos is a dream come true. It’s a team I’ve looked up to since I was young, and to now be part of such a successful and respected organisation is incredibly special," said Sheehan on the team's website.

"I believe I still have so much more to achieve in my career, and having the backing of this team is the perfect next step for me.

"I’m excited to get started, set ambitious goals and give everything I have to help the team win, while continuing to push myself to become the best rider I can be."

Sheehan joins Clément Champoussin, Harold Tejada, James Shaw, Joe Blackmore, Markel Beloki, and Benjamín Noval as new arrivals, as the once-dominant British WorldTour team looks to build a squad that can compete year-round.

"Riley is an exciting rider. He’s fast, technically very skilled and has the ability to perform across a range of terrain," Geraint Thomas, the team's Director of Racing said.

"We see him being a great addition to our Classics group, but he’s also a rider who can contribute right across the calendar. He brings plenty of versatility to the team, and we’re looking forward to helping him continue to develop."

With his arrival, Netcompany Ineos' roster is now up to 20 confirmed riders for the coming season, with Filippo Ganna as the headline departure, but also with three of Sheehan's US compatriots on the way out: Artem Shmidt, Magnus Sheffield, and AJ August.

Dave Brailsford's team are expected to close out their maximum of 30 names with a mixture of yet-to-be-announced contract extensions and further new arrivals.

items.title: Track World Championships: Great Britain reclaim women's team pursuit title, Bostock wins Scratch Race
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Denmark dominated the men's Team Pursuit, besting Italy, while the British team took home the bronze over France.

Matthew Bostock gave Britain their second gold of the night, topping Tom Sexton (New Zealand) in the Men's Scratch Race.

In the Men's Keirin, Harrie Lavreysen (Netherlands) took home his fifth rainbow jersey in the event and the country's second gold after the team sprint on Wednesday.

Read on for more details on how the races unfolded.

After breaking the world record earlier this year, Great Britain returned to their former perch as world champions in the Team Pursuit with a commanding victory thanks to defeats of the Netherlands and Italy.

After qualifying fastest on Wednesday, GB beat the Netherlands by more than three seconds in their semi-final, and then made it look even easier in the final as they beat last year's world champions Italy by more than five seconds.

Their final-winning time was 4:04.610, which was just under two seconds off their world-record time set at altitude at the European Championships in February.

Italy actually started the faster of the two teams in the final but they simply couldn't sustain their pace ands after dragging themselves into the green by the half-way mark, GB eased clear in the second half of the race, catching sight of the Italians down the straights as they re-claimed the title they won in 2023 and 2024.

Erin Boothman, Anna Morris, Millie Couzens, and Josie Knight were the quartet that rode the final for Great Britain, with Boothman swapping in for Megan Barker, who rode the semi-final. All five received gold medals.

The bronze medal went to Germany, who edged out the Netherlands in the match for third place. The Germany quartet was made up of Mieke Kröger, Lisa Klein, Message Bräutigam, and Franziska Brouße.

Denmark maintained their dominance in the men's Team Pursuit, clinching a fourth successive world title with a storming ride on Thursday.

Despite missing out on medals at the last Olympics in Paris in 2024, the Danes have solidified their status with a remarkable run that follows their world-record-breaking ride earlier this year at the European Championships.

Having qualified fastest and then seen off the Olympic champions Australia in a perfect start on Wednesday, the Danes finished the job in style on Thursday with victory over Italy in the final. They made a strong start and never let up, taking half a second after just two laps and extending it to two seconds just past the halfway mark.

Dropping down to three riders, they held their shape and smoothness all the way to the finish, stopping the clock on 3:40.865, only a shade off the world record of 3:39.977 they set at altitude in February.

Lasse Norman Leth, Carl-Frederik-Bévort, Frederik Madsen, and Rasmus Pedersen were the quartet that brought in the gold for Denmark. The Italian squad that took silver was a strong one, featuring Filippo Ganna, Jonathan Milan, Francesco Lamon, and Alessio Magagnotti.

The bronze medal went to Great Britain, who comfortably beat France in the match for third place.

Men's Team Pursuit Final Results

Lotte Kopecky (Belgium) claimed the ninth world title of her career with viceroy in the Elimination Race on Thursday.

The 30-year-old kept her cool throughout and in the end eased clear to an utterly one-sided victory on the final lap over Yumi Kajihara (Japan). The bronze medal went to Megan Jastrab (USA).

It was a disrupted race, with two stoppages, the latter after Kajihara hit the deck with just five riders remaining on the track. The race was neutralised briefly; Kajihara was allowed to return, and the Japanese woman went on to see off Valentine Fortin (France), Alyssa Polites (Australia), and Jastrab.

But by the final lap she had nothing left, and as Kopecky powered decisively away at the bell, she sat up and admitted defeat.

This is Koepcky's third world title in the Elimination Race, which she won in 2022 and 2023. She also has gold medals in the Madison and Points Race on the track, as well as two world titles in the road race, the last of which came in 2024.

Ahead of the women's Team Pursuit finals, the men's Scratch Race was the penultimate event of the day, and saw another gold medal for Great Britain as Matt Bostock stormed to a solo victory.

The 29-year-old claimed the biggest win of his career thanks to a brilliant attack with 12 laps of the 40 remaining. He took three laps to catch the solo leader Alex Vogel (Switzerland) and dispatched him immediately in one bend, going on to ride the last eight laps alone.

Riders gave chase in ones and twos during the initial phase of Bostock's attack but the peloton then bunched up and sat up, allowing Bostock to sail into an insurmountable lead with five laps remaining. With three to go, he was almost on the back of the bunch, and he coasted home in the final couple of laps to win by half a lap.

The Olympic champion was only second in his quarter-final heat but otherwise dominated the competition, and was a strong winner in a relatively close final. He came up on the outside to hit the front as the bell sounded, and he had the strength to hold off the rest.

items.title: 'Fourth place almost feels like a small victory' - Fabio Jakobsen starts to bounce back in Guangxi
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Once one of the world’s preeminent sprinters, winning bunch kicks in a variety of races and topping the points classification in the 2021 Vuelta a España, the 30-year-old former Dutch champion has a total of 46 wins to his name.

However, in recent years the Visma-Lease a Bike rider has regressed into a shadow of his former self, with his most recent victory as far back as April 2024. Thursday’s result was his best WorldTour placing since the UAE Tour in February of that year.

Suffering illnesses and injury, including iliac artery endofibrosis, Jakobsen was often unable to finish races, let alone contest the sprint, and while his results were tailing off towards the end of his time with Soudal-QuickStep, his loss of form coincided with a move to what is now Picnic-Post NL.

In more than four years with the team, he managed only one victory. However, a mid-season move to Visma over the summer seems to have sparked something in Jakobsen.

Since joining the team on August 14th, he has won two national-level races and has begun clawing his way up results boards, drawing praise from his sports director in Guangxi, Gaëton Pons.

"This fourth place almost feels like a small victory when you consider where Fabio has come from," Pons said. "In his last four races with the team, he has achieved his four best results of the season. Physically, he's not back to his previous level yet, but we're clearly seeing progress. He wants to fight again, enjoys racing, and is showing a lot of confidence. That's an important step toward next season."

Seeing Jakobsen slipping out the back of the bunch whenever the road tilted uphill had become a sad but familiar sight, so the team hadn’t identified Thursday’s 212.3km stage, which included almost 1,800m of climbing, as one for him, but he defied expectations, playing a full part in the final.

"He managed to survive the climbs thanks to the support of his teammates. In the finale, the guys did an excellent job. Fabio himself mentioned that it had been a long time since he'd had such a good lead-out. Owain [Doull], in particular, did a fantastic job in the final meters."

Friday’s stage is hillier, and Jakobsen is highly unlikely to be able to fight for the win, though Saturday’s fifth stage could present another chance.

items.title: Eneco Tour: Jakob Söderqvist doubles up with dominant stage 2 time trial victory, extends race lead
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) doubled up on victories at the Eneco Tour, adding the stage 2 individual time trial to his prologue success in the Netherlands on Thursday.

In a close-fought battle over the flat 13.6km course in Tilburg, Finn Fisher-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) had set the best time and held off a powerful charge from Ethan Hayter (Soudal-QuickStep) by less than half a second, but the Swedish rider was simply too fast and knocked him off the hot seat as the last starter.

Almost crashing as getting on the power too early caused him to pedal strike around one of the final corners, Söderqvist stayed up and arrived at the line in a time of 15:04 to beat Fisher-Black by 11 seconds, also the only rider to average more than 54kph throughout his effort.

With a small hop over the line, the Swede netted the eighth win of his career and sixth in a time trial as a professional, also extending his overall lead of the race to 14 seconds from Hayter and 15 from Fisher-Black.

"It was a fast one, actually; I think I experienced it faster than I expected beforehand. I didn't feel too much headwind even though we were talking about it a lot before, so it was just a good day, and I cannot say much more than that," said Söderqvist.

"It was nice corners, kept you on your toes a bit – how I like it – and it was a bigger pleasure than normally."

He'll look to defend his orange jersey in the remaining three stages, with punchy routes and some likely breathless racing standing in his way of the overall title on Sunday. Sat in eighth overall, 29 seconds down, Christophe Laporte (Visma-Lease a Bike) looks the most likely rider to challenge Söderqvist for the overall.

"For sure I'm happy. Everything so far is as good as we could ever expect. I was strong in this race also last year, so we know it suits me really well, but I'm happy the shape is still here with me this time of year, and we hope to keep it," he said.

"The pressure will be on, and we know how good people like Christophe Laporte are on Vam Berg," who won his European title there in 2023, "and even tomorrow will already be a lot of pressure from the other teams who believe. We are here to fight, and this is how we need to pursue."

Racing continued at the Eneco Tour with Milan De Ceuster (Picnic PostNL) leading the 87 riders off the start ramp of the stage 2 individual time trial in reverse GC order.

An early benchmark was set by Steffen De Schuyteneer (Lotto Intermarché) with a time of 15:46 over the 13.6-kilometre course in Tilburg, until he was beaten by Milan Lanhove (Team Flanders-Baloise), who went eight seconds quicker.

As a result of the opening day's prologue, most of the top time trial riders were placed inside the top 10 on GC, so Lanhove would have known his time was vulnerable, and it was Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) who knocked him off the hot seat by 11 seconds – but there were several riders going even faster on the course.

Among those ahead of Campenaerts at the intermediate check were his Visma teammate Edoardo Affini and Kristian Egholm (Lidl-Trek Future Racing), but both lost out by more than 10 seconds after a rapid final run to the line by the Belgian.

Pepijn Reinderink (Soudal Quick-Step) was the first rider to average more than 53kph over the course, knocking Campenaerts out of the top spot, with just eight riders still to come in. But it wasn't long before Fisher-Black scorched to the line four seconds quicker than the Dutchman.

Hayter ran him close, missing out on the lead by less than half a second, but the prologue winner and pre-stage favourite Söderqvist was powering through the course, clocking through the intermediate check five seconds faster than the Kiwi.

Söderqvist ramped up his speed and the risk, almost coming unstuck before the final kilometre, but he kept it together to convincingly beat everyone by more than 10 seconds.

items.title: 'It became a dictatorship' – Extensive report on alleged culture of fear leads Picnic-PostNL to launch independent investigation
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
WorldTour team Picnic PostNL will commission an "independent, professional investigation into our team culture" after an extensive report in Dutch media revealed alleged toxic working conditions in recent years, which one former coach described as a "dictatorship".

revealed the findings of their investigative report on Thursday morning, conducted over several months in 2026, into the culture that developed under sports director Rudi Kemna and team owner Iwan Spekenbrink.

The two media outlets spoke with 71 current or former employees of the team, most of them being quoted anonymously, to paint a picture of an alleged "culture of fear" and an "unsafe working situation".

Picnic-PostNL issued a statement on Thursday, saying "we do not recognise ourselves in the overall picture presented in the publications", but nevertheless acknowledging that "it is important to take a critical look at ourselves" in light of the reported findings.

"The fact that experiences differ does not diminish the seriousness of the accounts that have now come to light. We will therefore commission an independent investigation into how our team culture is experienced in practice and to what extent it reflects the culture we strive for," read the statement.

"We will take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may be needed, out of respect for everyone who is, or has been, part of Team Picnic PostNL."

What exactly has been said about the culture in the team?

The most striking claim of a toxic culture came from retired professional rider Martijn Tusveld, who raced in the team's colours for seven seasons, first as Sunweb and then as DSM between 2018 and 2024. He highlighted how his standing in the team changed when – after being asked for his opinion by Kemna – he openly criticised the team's tactics at the Giro d'Italia in 2020.

Tusveld was reportedly told he was creating a "negative atmosphere" and would later tell Kemna directly, in a 2025 email, that after the Giro incident he no longer dared to speak up, feeling "powerless", and even that he was not the person he once was.

"I became anxious," he told . "I thought: I'll keep my mouth shut and say yes and amen. And that's what I did for the rest of the years with this team."

Tusveld also said he suffered with symptoms of depression in 2021, stating: "I also thought about harming myself."

Just one account of the 71, similar experiences to Tusveld's about a shift in the team's culture were detailed by anonymous former staff members in the report.

Tom Dumoulin's former coach Adriaan Helmantel was another who spoke on the record, claiming that Dumoulin's landmark victory at the Giro d'Italia in 2017 did mark a turning point for the team, but not in the way it should have.

As Helmantel saw it, the management looked to exert excessive influence, wanting everything to trickle down from the top, as "they started becoming paranoid" of riders "calling the shots" if riders and coaches became too close.

"It became a dictatorship," Helmantel said.

In a separate report from , former rider Nicolas Roche, who also rode for Team Sky and Saxo Bank, issued a striking statement: "I think this management is not suitable for cycling," said the Irishman.

"In cycling, we have to deal with a lot of variables. It is not a predictable sport. The body is not a perfect machine. We have to deal with the weather conditions and also the tactics of 24 other teams. I understand that people want a master plan to be prepared, but they cannot plan the 17th stage of the Tour de France as early as May. And that is what they did."

Roche claimed that he was "pushed towards the exit" in 2021 and that he was told he had "too much influence on the young riders", stating: "My experience became a problem for the management."

In their statement, Picnic-PostNL said: "If people have felt unsafe within our organisation or have felt they lacked sufficient opportunity to raise concerns, we want to understand how that could have happened."

Team dispute claims they didn't engage with investigation

While Picnic-PostNL have now issued a statement and vowed to launch an internal investigation in direct response to the report from and they have disputed the two publications' claims that they refused to engage with the investigation.

claim that they approached the team for comment in response to their findings on October 12, and then approached the team management in-person two days later, stating: " and gave owner Iwan Spekenbrink the opportunity at the Picnic-PostNL headquarters in Deventer to respond regarding the WorldTour team's working methods. Spekenbrink proved unwilling to do so and ultimately chose not to respond at all. Neither in writing nor on camera."

Picnic PostNL have a differing view on how attempts at conversation played out once presented with the investigation, as referenced in their statement.

"According to , it spent months trying to speak with current and former riders and staff members. As soon as we received indications that the investigation was taking place, we offered to meet with to discuss our philosophy and vision, and to give the broadcaster the opportunity to speak with current team members and colleagues. NOS chose not to take up that offer. We regret this.

"Last Monday, we were then given only a few days to respond to a number of questions, either in writing or on camera. In response, we made several further attempts to speak with . These attempts were unsuccessful."

Picnic-PostNL's statement in full

We have taken note of the publications by NOS Sport and In de Waaier about Team Picnic PostNL. The accounts shared by current and former riders and staff members affect us. At the same time, we do not recognise ourselves in the overall picture presented in the publications.

The fact that experiences differ does not diminish the seriousness of the accounts that have now come to light. We will therefore commission an independent investigation into how our team culture is experienced in practice and to what extent it reflects the culture we strive for.

The team and our three promises

Since the team was founded in 2008, three promises have formed the foundation of our approach to professional cycling.

The first promise: fair, healthy and responsible sport.

Our anti-doping policy is an important part of this promise. It is not only about what we communicate externally, but also about the mindset and ethical considerations that guide our decisions in practice.

The second promise: safe collaboration based on shared values.

We want everyone within the team, on and off the bike, to be treated with respect and to feel free to express an opinion, encourage one another, ask questions and raise concerns. Mutual commitment and integrity are central to this, helping us create an environment where people can develop, perform and enjoy working together.

The third promise: continuity and job security.

We have made a commitment to do everything we can to secure the future of the team and, in doing so, preserve jobs within professional cycling.

While this may sound self-evident, job security in professional cycling is anything but. The sport’s economic model falls seriously short. Every year, several teams disappear, with the associated loss of jobs. This has become almost normal, even though it should never be the case in a sport of this scale.

That is why we have been working to secure the future of the team since 2008. Over the years, we have provided employment for hundreds of people.

According to NOS, it spent months trying to speak with current and former riders and staff members. As soon as we received indications that the investigation was taking place, we offered to meet with NOS to discuss our philosophy and vision, and to give the broadcaster the opportunity to speak with current team members and colleagues. NOS chose not to take up that offer. We regret this.

Last Monday, we were then given only a few days to respond to a number of questions, either in writing or on camera. In response, we made several further attempts to speak with NOS. These attempts were unsuccessful.

Independent investigation into team culture

In a performance-driven environment such as professional sport, things can go wrong. That is why there are several ways for people within our team to raise problems and concerns. Riders have a personal coach, there is a Rider Committee, and staff members can turn to confidential advisers. If people have felt unsafe within our organisation or have felt they lacked sufficient opportunity to raise concerns, we want to understand how that could have happened.

We are proud of what we have built since 2008 together with the many people who are, or have been, part of and associated with this team. Precisely for that reason, we believe it is important to take a critical look at ourselves.

We will therefore commission an independent, professional investigation into our team culture. We will take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may be needed, out of respect for everyone who is, or has been, part of Team Picnic PostNL.

items.title: Should you rethink the cycling kit you're buying? Why circularity could be the future of sustainable clothing
items.author: Emma Cole
items.content:
According to the European Environment Agency (EEA), each European citizen throws away an average of 16kg of textiles each year. The EEA estimates almost 75% of this is incinerated or ends up in landfill, and some is shipped to Asia and Africa.

The reality of this is shocking. I’ve seen it first-hand at markets in Tunisia where hundreds of tables of clothing are piled high and sold for a few pounds, and global fast fashion brands do the same thing but on a much, much bigger scale around the world.

Albeit smaller than the big fast fashion manufacturers, cycling clothing is also part of this conversation, especially given the constant flow of new collection launches, designs and colourways.

The UN Environment Programme says 2-8% of CO2 emissions come from the textile industry, while the Ellen MacArthur Foundation says that only 1% of clothing is circular.

Circularity refers to the concept of keeping clothing in use for as long as possible, through reuse, repair, and recycling, essentially a loop, and eliminating waste. By comparison, the traditional manufacturing model is linear: clothing is sold to be worn and then disposed of, often without regard for repair and reuse.

Circularity has yet to become mainstream in the clothing industry, let alone the cycling kit sector, but French brand Velor is trying to change that. We spoke to Velor and other voices in the cycling industry to learn more about the future of sustainable clothing, and how cyclists can join that movement.

A world-first 'circular' cycling jersey

Velor, a brand founded in France in 2021, has created the first circular cycling jersey made from textile waste, could represent a major step forward for both the sportswear and textile industries. It took five years from concept to bringing the jersey to market, because Velor had to build every step from scratch.

"We started from nothing, and we had to build it ourselves," says Florian Jardin, who co-founded Velor with his brother Mickael.

"The whole value chain is very complicated because you start with low volumes, you grow step by step, and it's not standard fabrics."

The brand’s supply chain starts in France and the Netherlands with clothing collection, and heads through France, Germany, Spain, and Portugal for the final product, before closing the loop by returning to the collection stage.

Velor scaled its circular jersey gradually, from lab-testing a single jersey, to recycling 300 jerseys two years ago, to now processing at the one-tonne scale.

The brand also worked with Maastricht University and its suppliers to understand the impact of its jersey and to quantify the life cycle assessment data. Jardin says the result is an infinitely recyclable jersey, made from 85% textile waste and a footprint of 0.9kg CO2 equivalent.

"If you look at a jersey made in China, the emissions are 3-4kg for an equivalent jersey with the same fabric, weight and construction," he adds.

Another non-traditional business model is using a pre-order system, which requires customers to wait for their kit to be made, but allows brands to produce only as much as they need.

Bristol-based brand Kostüme produces kits solely via pre-order. Founder Ed Bartlett says a pre-order model removes the waste which is baked into the traditional retail model.

"A lot of brands are trying to solve the wrong part of the problem by focusing on recycled fabrics and repair capabilities, but the problem is we're making too much stuff," says Bartlett.

"The research that I've done suggests 30% of products get sold at full price, 30% get sold at a discount, 40% don't ever get sold, and then a lot of brands have a 40% return rate, so even the stuff that they're selling gets returned, and these are big numbers.

"If you can cut that by even 10% or 20%, that has a much bigger impact than anything else."

Bartlett says his 55% returning customer rate and 100% year-on-year growth are proof that the pre-order model works.

Kostüme also doesn’t carry the cost of unsold stock which gives Bartlett flexibility. For example, Kostüme’s bib shorts use a separately applied gripper that adds two weeks to production time and costs more but virtually eliminates fabric waste.

The few items that aren't sold or are returned go to their Ready to Ship store, offering customers a chance to buy an item with a faster turn around time.

Swiss brand Assos recently tested the pre-order model through a jersey collaboration with One Garment at a Time (OGAT).

"The OGAT project was a way to test a new business model that brings us closer to the customer, letting us plan and produce with the goal of zero waste and zero excess stock," says Davide Colletto, quality, safety and environment manager at Assos.

"It is a more sustainable approach, and we are evaluating how this model could be extended to other parts of our range where it makes sense."

Why aren’t more brands trying to close the loop and reduce waste?

In the early days of Velor, Jardin reached out to many of the major brands in the hope of partnering with them, but he didn’t get much engagement.

"I spoke to all of them, but they said they weren’t interested, didn’t have time or it wasn’t in their strategy," he says.

He says cost was also a reason. Producing circular fabric costs about 11 times more than sourcing fabric from China, while manufacturing in Portugal costs five to six times more than in China, according to Jardin.

Jardin built these costs into the business from the start, but for bigger brands there would be a large cost for them to pivot their business model.

"The circular economy needs to deliver cheap products, and that means scaling up and getting the economies of scale", says Dr Sam Hampton, a lecturer and researcher in Environmental Governance and Behaviour Energy programme at the University of Oxford.

But, as Velor shows, that doesn’t exist yet.

Dr Hampton suggests a carbon tax on virgin raw materials which could be a lever to make recycled alternatives comparatively cheaper.

"You need to change the whole system in multiple ways, make the virgin competitors more expensive and the recycled competitive products cheaper, but that's a system-wide global challenge."

The domination of the traditional model means pivoting is difficult.

"The linear model still dominates the industry, but it's becoming harder to justify environmentally, commercially and in regulation," says Sam Wrest, senior ESG manager at Rapha.

"Circularity is the direction we're moving in, but in cycling apparel it comes with real technical challenges."

The technical challenges revolve around the difficulties of recycling mixed materials.

"Cycling kit relies on elastane blends, bonded seams, silicone grippers and chamois pads, which are very hard to recycle back into new fibre," explains Wrest. "Textile-to-textile recycling for these materials isn't commercially viable at scale yet."

Wrest says Rapha is exploring this area nonetheless, and expects to share more soon, but its current focus remains on durability, repairs and its trade-in service to extend the lives of existing garments. Danish brand Pas Normal Studios echoes these challenges.

"Right now, the most effective lever within our control is keeping products in use for longer, through quality, repairs and spare parts," says Fabian Pirrwitz, Impact and responsibility analyst at Pas Normal Studios.

Moving to mono-material – garments made exclusively of one fabric – is also not a straightforward solution, particularly not when it comes to technical or high-performance cycling clothing.

"Mono-material fabrics can make recycling easier, but the recycling and recovery infrastructure is still limited and not yet fully developed," adds Colletto of Assos.

"Different garments have different technical requirements, and a single material is not always the best way to achieve the performance, comfort and durability we need."

The challenges don't stop there, either. There is also the issue of synthetic fibres shedding microplastics during washing, and the long-term impact of things like PFAs, which were previously used extensively in cycling clothing and waterproofs. Whilst many brands are trying, the task of making cycling clothing sustainable and environmentally friendly is far from simple.

While Velor and Kostüme openly talk about their supply chains, some brands shy away from transparency over where your clothes come from and how they are made.

Several mainstream cycling brands operate with supply chains in China and Vietnam. Maap, Decathlon (Van Rysel) and Rapha manufacture some products in Asia.

Decathlon brand Van Rysel has removed carbon emissions information from its website for many of its jerseys, and some of its latest products don’t have any environmental initiatives linked to them, giving the impression that the brand is scaling back on its transparency and sustainability.

One Decathlon jersey still listed with emissions comes in at 4.9kg CO2 equivalent. We approached Van Rysel for comment, but did not receive a response in time for publication.

An upcoming EU regulation called the Digital Product Passport (DPP) scheme could change this lack of transparency in the world of cycling clothing. The DPP will require all textiles sold in the EU to include data across supply chains such as material, chemicals, origin, and recyclability. It is expected to apply by the end of 2029.

"I think what we need is more transparency… A name and a company for every step of the process," says Jardin.

Fabric certifications such as Bluesign and OEKO-TEX are often used to imply sustainability credentials, but they're not the be-all and end-all, and certainly don't cover all factors of production.

"A certified fabric doesn't tell you a brand's overall carbon footprint, the full picture of how workers are treated, or what happens to products when they reach the end of their life," says Wrest.

"Certifications are useful for managing specific risks in the supply chain, but they're a starting point, not proof of sustainability."

A more circular and less wasteful future?

With the recent record-breaking heatwaves and ongoing climate crisis, it would be logical for consumer habits to change – not just as shoppers all wake up to the impact that unsustainable consumption and business practices can have on the world around, but in response to climate change itself.

Dr Hampton predicts a drive for new lighter summer kit which performs in the heat, rather than less buying overall, for example.

For traditional business models, upcoming regulation will force them to pivot to more transparent practices, but the costs of going circular and lack of recycling infrastructure remain significant hurdles for many brands.

However, Velor’s innovation with an infinitely recyclable jersey shows us what is possible and showcases how a circular clothing economy could work.

Similarly, Kostüme’s business success highlights a consumer desire for a different way of thinking, but both Kostüme and Velor are small parts of a much wider and impactful cycling clothing ecosystem.

"We’re a drop in the ocean ultimately, but hopefully we can scale this to a point where it’s inarguable, and people can’t shy away from it," says Bartlett.

But with major player Assos testing the waters with pre-order, and Rapha focusing on garment longevity, perhaps the future of cycling clothing is a little bit rounder after all.

items.title: Eneco Tour Women: Lieke Nooijen flies to second time trial win on stage 2 and retakes overall lead
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Lieke Nooijen blasted to a second time trial stage win of the Eneco Tour Women on Thursday, overcoming some fierce competition in the stage 2 test in the Dutch town of Tilburg.

The Visma-Lease a Bike rider was the only competitor to stop the clock under 16 minutes over the 13.1km course, with Nienke Vinke (SD Worx-Protime) second, more than 20 seconds down, while stage 1 winner Sandrine Tas (Lotto-Intermarché) was third, a further second back.

Nooijen won the opening day’s prologue TT on Tuesday and now leads the GC standings, 20 seconds ahead of Tas, with Vinke third, with three stages left to race.

Nooijen has established herself as one of the best time trialists in the peloton this year and in this company was the clear favourite to win on Thursday. However, she will need to defend her lead on the ensuing stages, all of which have short punchy climbs, though the advantage she has built may well prove enough for her to take the overall come Sunday.

Nooijen had Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) not far in front as her carrot to chase, admitting that "Yes, of course, it always gives more motivation to beat her, and she was in front of me and came closer, but I didn’t catch her.

"It was hard, but I’m super happy to take my second victory on the TT bike here, and I had a lot of confidence since the time of the prologue," said Nooijen, with her eye on carrying the orange jersey all the way to the end.

"[There are] still three days to go. Also hard stages, so I think we can make a nice plan with our strong team, and also tomorrow it will be hard in Limburg, and then on Saturday on the Vam Berg, but you need to be sharp the whole race."

For its third day of racing, the Eneco Tour Women took on a 13.1km ITT effort with only 27m of elevation gain, almost completely flat, with a decent wind of around 15kph that was rarely at the riders’ back, though only with the first three kilometres into a full headwind.

First off the ramp was Austrian TT champion Christina Schweinberger, the Fenix-Premier Tech rider setting a time of 7:54 at the intermediate coming point and a finish time of 17:41. Second rider off was British new pro Robyn Clay (Picnic-PostNL), who stopped the clock just seven seconds slower than the Austrian, the two riders staying in first and second place respectively for some time.

Eventually Tess Moerman (AG Insurance-Soudal) overtook Clay before Slovakian champion Viktória Chladoňová (Visma-Lease a Bike) managed to usurp Schweinberger, having started as the 55th of the day’s 88 starters.

However, Chaladoňová was just the first of a number of faster times, with Silke Smulders (Liv-AlUla-Jayco), Femke De Vries (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Vinke all spending a while in the race lead until Nooijen overtook them all for victory.

items.title: Conflicting reports surrounding the inclusion of the Montmartre climb on the final stage of the 2027 Tour de France route
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Editor's note: This article has been updated to reflect subsequent reports published in the French press.

Question marks have emerged concerning the future of the punchy Montmartre circuit that has shaken up the final stage of the Tour de France in the past two years, with conflicting reports in the French press surrounding its inclusion on the 2027 Tour de France route.

The route for the 2027 Tour de France will be unveiled in Paris next Thursday, and the newspaper reported this Thursday morning that the Montmartre climb is set to be excluded, meaning a return to a traditional flat-track sprint finish on the Champs Elysées.

However, this was later contradicted by separate reports from and , with both outlets reporting that the Classics-flavoured finale will be back for a third year of high drama and entertainment.

In the past two years, the Côte de la Butte Montmartre has shaken up the traditional format of the Tour's finale, measuring 1.1 km at an average gradient of 5.9%, mostly on cobblestones, and followed by a tricky little descent.

The organisers had already tweaked the format, extending the distance from the top of the climb to the finish line from six kilometres to just over 10km, which resulted in the closer contest between the attackers and the sprinters.

This appeared to strike a better balance between tradition and the modern desire for action and entertainment.

However, both editions were somewhat awkward, given that general classification timings have been neutralised on both occasions, with the GC 'frozen' and therefore finalised upon entry to the final circuit.

The final stage of the Tour has for many years been processional, with riders drinking champagne and posing for photographs in the early kilometres before racing in central Paris, but any situation where proper GC racing could see positions – or even the yellow jersey – change hands, would throw that celebratory atmosphere up in the air.

The last bunch sprint on the Champs Elysées came in 2023, with the 2024 edition moved from Paris entirely due to the Olympics taking place in the French capital that summer, and the Tour ending with a time trial in Nice.

It remains to be seen what the organisers do with stage 21 in the long-run, but more will become clear when we see what is officially confirmed for the final day of the 2027 Tour next Thursday.

items.title: Tour of Guangxi: Milan Fretin pips Biesterbos to stage 3 victory after well-placed Paul Magnier unclips during sprint
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
Milan Fretin (Cofidis) sped to victory on stage 3 of the Tour of Guangxi, claiming the longest stage of the race in a messy sprint ahead of stage 2 winner Frits Biesterbos (Picnic PostNL).

With the finish line on a wide road into Bama, the sprint was spread all across the road with little room for organisation, and most sprinters in the wind early and making a desperate dash for the line.

Powering up the right-hand side of the road, Fretin just held Biesterbos off to claim the win, with Jordi Meeus (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) grabbing third. Fabio Jakobsen (Visma-Lease a Bike) had his best sprint of the week so far to take fourth.

Stage 1 winner Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) had the best lead-out, dropped off just 150m from the line, but as he opened up his sprint he pulled his right foot out of his pedal and lost all speed. He was swamped by the pack and left banging his handlebars in frustration as he crossed the line in 21st.

Magnier's misfortune and Biesterbos' second place means that the Dutchman now takes over the lead of the race, donning the red jersey on Thursday, though a hilly day on stage 4 means he probably won't hold onto it for long.

Though it finished in a sprint, stage 3 from Jingxi to Bama was an undulating and long 212km day, with four climbs in the final 60km as the difficulty began to ramp up in China.

A three-man breakaway of Jasha Sütterlin (Jayco AlUla), Tobias Bayer (Alpecin-Premier Tech) and Wang Ruidong (China) went away early in the stage, with Wang's efforts in the climbs earning him the KoM jersey.

Despite the profile of the final part of the stage looking ripe for attacks, it wasn't quite as aggressive as it could have been, with the leaders not caught until 20km to go with Wang valiantly pushing on solo to be the final escapee.

From there, Soudal-QuickStep and Decathlon CMA CGM kept the pace high and controlled enough to discourage any attacks and keep things together for their desired bunch sprint – though ultimately both teams got little for their efforts, with Magnier's incident costing him, and Olav Kooij not able to contest the sprint.

The Tour of Guangxi kicks up a notch tomorrow, with four categorised climbs and many more uncategorised ascents on a day that takes in over 2,700m of climbing before a downhill finish into Tian'e.

items.title: Monumental year takes US rising star Ashlin Barry from 'I could barely walk' to 'memory that will last a lifetime'
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
New under-23 road world champion Ashlin Barry didn't have a lot of time to celebrate a gold medal and a rainbow jersey as one of the most extraordinary rewards for a 19th birthday three weeks ago. After his solo conquest across the slopes of Mont Royal in the U23 road race at the UCI Road World Championships, he went straight to Los Angeles for a training camp on the track with Team USA and then headed to Shanghai for the UCI Track World Championships.

There's no time to rest on any laurels for Barry, as his sights are set on a version of California dreaming at the Los Angeles Olympic Games, now 639 days away.

"At the moment, I'm putting a lot of focus on the track in Team Pursuit, and then maybe qualifying for the Omnium, or something will come as a byproduct of that. If I could qualify for the road [at the Olympic Games], that would be pretty cool. But I think I have to take a step up physically from where I am now to make that selection," Barry told in an exclusive one-on-one interview in Montréal.

"In terms of preparation, there's a lot going into our team pursuit now, and whether it's like a bunch event on the track or qualifying for the road, I think those will fall into place."

Barry has a huge balancing act to manage across multiple disciplines, global travel and a new commitment through 2029 to the Visma-Lease a Bike Development squad that could see him jump to the WorldTour team sooner rather than later.

Just two years before, he impressed with a silver medal in the Omnium at the Junior Track World Championships, sweeping US national titles in the road race and time trial, and winning junior and elite national titles in the Madison.

In 2025, after graduating from high school, he came second in the junior men's E3 Saxo Classic and Paris-Roubaix, earned a silver medal in the junior time trial at World Roads and the gold medal in the US Pro junior time trial national championships.

But his plan to make a statement on the track was derailed at the start of 2026, and he kept goals with his new Visma team modest.

"This was a tough year because I was supposed to do Pan Am Championships in February. I crashed on my knee in January, so I wasn't able to ride my bike. I could barely walk," he recalled.

"Things didn't go as planned. I was in Spain at training camp. Then I had to get some stitches in my knee, and I couldn't bend it. It could have been a lot worse, but it was a couple of weeks off the bike, and then I missed the track because of that."

While his track maturation was put on hold in the spring, he jumped into the fray in the Olympia's Tour at the end of March, earning two podiums. He then finished fifth in the U23 In Flanders Fields and then won the US Pro U23 road race and came in fourth in the US Pro elite men's road race the next day.

So when he finished one step off the podium in the U23 time trial at Montreal Road Worlds, he had modest expectations yet again. When asked two days before the U23 road race what he expected, the teen simply stated that he could be competitive on Friday but was "not going in thinking I have a super-high chance of getting a medal".

A gold medal and rainbow jersey were the result of a solo ride on his biggest stage yet. Barry called the win in the men's U23 road race "a memory that will last a lifetime". It was a monumental final 30 kilometres of the 174km contest, as the teenager carried the colours of Team USA to the win, and enthralled family and friends from two countries as a dual citizen of the US and Canada.

Even as he held his pace at the front of the race for the 12th of 13 circuits across Mont Royal, he said he wasn't sure he was strong enough to maintain a 40-second advantage. However, once he crested the major climb the final time and added to his solo lead, he let himself believe he could win, encouraged by supporters around the course.

"Once I was away, I just committed. It really felt like a home race out there," he told the media, including , in Montreal. "It was just unreal being out there, seeing so many friends, seeing my family. I could hear my dog barking on the side of the course."

He now registers an entry in the family's journal of success in Montreal, his mother and former US elite women's road race national champion Dede Demet-Barry having won a pro race in Montreal in 2002, five years before Barry was born. His father and two-time Canadian road race silver medallist Michael Barry competed on the Mont Royal course on two editions of Grand Prix du Cycliste Montreal, when his son was old enough to remember ringing a cowbell at his father's race.

Both parents competed at multiple road world championships for their respective countries; Michael's best effort was eighth in the U23 road race in 1996, while Dede won the junior road title in 1989. And Dede also competed frequently on the track, going fourth at the UCI Junior World Track Championships.

Demet-Barry later translated that speed to a silver medal on the road at the Athens Olympic Games in the individual time trial. An Olympic medal of any colour, and in road or track, has the attention of her son.

Barry said one of the reasons he enjoys the track so much is the emphasis on teamwork, be it Team Pursuit and other events like Madison. In fact, his personal favourite moment from 2025 was not even a win, but a fourth-place finish.

"[Last year] at Track Worlds, we were just off the cusp of getting a medal. But seeing the way that programme's come together has been really cool, and I'm personally proud to be a part of it, proud of those guys and seeing the way they've improved," he said about the US Men's Team Pursuit squad.

"[Track] Worlds will be a really good opportunity for me, and then I'm hoping next year to do Track Worlds again, hoping to get some more racing experience on the track."

This year, the quest for a gold medal in Team Pursuit began on the first day of the 2026 UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai as Barry rejoined Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson with the new addition of Taylor Phinney. They made it through qualifying but not the first round, with France ending their dreams. Barry will race the individual pursuit and Elimination Race later this week.

On the road, before earning his world title, Barry said his top road highlight of the season also showed the teamwork he values.

"There's something special about achieving something with another person or with a group of people, and being able to share that moment. The Olympia story comes to mind. That was just a cool moment, I mean one-two is cool," Barry said about that March race with teammates on the podium.

"We had a great team there. It's a good atmosphere; I really liked that course. I feel proud about the way that I raced there and worked with my teammate Aldo.

"My teammate and I were in that front gro,up and probably we had a pretty equal chance of winning, either one of us. I mean, he was second in the end, but he helped me set up that winning attack. He could have gone to the finish and won. It just ended by luck that I was the one winning."

Barry has the talent, not just the luck. Those two top moments of the past two seasons, however, were probably pushed to runner-up positions after he won the U23 road world championship.

In fact, his personal victory was also one for his country, scoring the country's first-ever U23 world title for a US athlete. And who was the last U23 men's rider to take a medal of any colour? It was his track teammate Taylor Phinney in 2010, who tied Canadian Guillaume Boivin to give the USA a bronze.

items.title: 'Same start time, same distance, same energy' - Charlotte Kool calls out Eneco Tour on unequal prize list
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
However, their focus on equity hasn't made its way to the prize purse, a point that sprint leader Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) pointed out on Instagram. She posted an image of the prize list, which shows the women are racing for a total of €17,205 while the men's purse is €63,465.

"I'm curious if women get a discount at @eneco for energy? Prologue: Same start time, same distance, same energy," Kool wrote in the post.

While men's prologue winner Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) pocketed €1,490 for his effort, women's winner Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) earned just €220. Tim Merlier (Soudal-Quickstep) will take home €3,060 for winning the sprint on stage 1, while Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché) gained just €370.

Speaking to Kool expanded, saying, "It's not about the money for us; that is just a small bonus. It's more about the principle, that it's a bit strange.

"It was a bit of a joke," she said of her post. "Because it is of course a bit skewed that, as the Eneco Tour, you promote that men and women are on equal footing, and then there is such a difference in prize money."

During the 2020 season, Flanders Classics, organisers of the Tour of Flanders and other races, launched an initiative called 'Closing the Gap' to bring more parity to broadcast coverage and prize money. The Tour of Flanders awarded equal prizes in 2022, and Flanders Classics extended that to five other races in 2023.

But events like the Tour de France still give women a tenth of what the men earn, so the fight is not over yet.

items.title: Netcompany Ineos sign 23-year-old former Tour de l'Avenir winner for 2027
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
The young British racer joins Ineos after two years at NSN and Israel-Premier Tech, which followed a dramatically successful 2024 season that saw him win both the Tour de l’Avenir and the U23 Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

This year, however, Blackmore's racing has been severely disrupted by knee injuries, to the point where he took part in just three races and abandoned all of them. He did, however, complete the Tour de France in his first full season as a pro back in 2025, when he also claimed fourth in Brabantse Pijl in the same year.

Blackmore was one of three signings announced by Ineos Grenadiers on Wednesday, the other two being fellow Briton James Shaw and French climber Clément Champoussin.

“I’m extremely excited and grateful for the opportunity to spend the next three years of my career with Netcompany Ineos," Blackmore said in a team press release.

"It’s been a tough 2026 for me with injuries, but it’s made me even more motivated to reach my full potential.

“Joe is a rider we’ve followed closely, and someone we believe has significant potential," Netcompany Ineos director of racing Geraint Thomas added.

"He has already shown what he is capable of across different types of racing, but importantly we believe there is still a lot more to come."

Shaw, 30, has yet to take a win in his career, but with seven Grand Tours in his palmares, the Briton has built a solid reputation as a strong climber. Shaw is also well known for setting his career back on track after two initial pro seasons at Lotto were followed by three away from the WorldTour in smaller squads.

At a point where others would have thrown in the towel, Shaw made it back to the top level and has now raced for the last five years at EF Education-EasyPost. “As a kid, this [Ineos] was the team that inspired me," Shaw said.

"I grew up looking up to riders like Geraint Thomas, so to now have the opportunity to pull on the jersey and become part of a team I've admired for so long is a dream come true."

Also set to provide a boost to Netcompany Ineos climbing line-up in 2027, like Shaw, is 28-year-old Clément Champoussin, moving on from XDS-Astana to race with the British WorldTour team next season.

A former top-ten finisher in Paris-Nice and Itzulia Basque Country, Champoussin has signed a three-year deal through to 2029 with Netcompany Ineos. They will be his fourth professional team following spells as AG2R-Decathlon, Arkéa-Samsic and, most recently, two years at Astana.

This year a promising early start for Champoussin, including a fifth place overall at Itzulia Basque Country and top 20 placings in La Flèche Wallonne and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, was followed by a more uneven midseason. 2026 was the first time since 2022 that the Frenchman has not taken part in a single Grand Tour, where his best placing remains 16th overall in the Vuelta back in 2021.

“Clément brings significant experience and another dimension to the group," Thomas added about the Frenchman, originally from Nice, but now reportedly a resident in Andorra.

"He's a solid, strong and consistent climber who has shown he can perform at the highest level.

In a busy transfer season for Netcompany Ineos, the British squad is set to see multiple significant departures and arrivals this winter. Amongst those departing are Italian time trial giant Filippo Ganna, Americans AJ August and Magnus Sheffield, British allrounder Ben Swift, who is retiring, and Australian sprinter Sam Welsford.

Meanwhile, Champoussin, Shaw and Blackmore are three of the seven riders currently confirmed to be heading the opposite direction, with others joining Ineos including Champoussin's current XDS-Astana teammate, Harold Tejada, and the teenage Spanish star and double junior World Champion, Benjamin Noval.

items.title: 'I was deliberately pushed into the barriers' – Guarischi relegated from Eneco Tour sprint after complaints from Kool
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Barbara Guarischi (SD Worx-Protime) has been relegated for her sprint on stage 1 of the Eneco Tour, after her actions left Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech), the rider she hampered in the final 150 metres, furious at the finish line on Wednesday.

Kool was the favourite for the flat stage in Ede, and was well placed on the wheel of the Italian rider coming out of the final corner. As Guarischi launched her sprint in the middle of the road, Kool began to launch on her left, only for the Italian rider to close her to the barrier, causing the Dutch rider to take evasive action and restart her sprint on the other side.

By the time she was back up to speed, Kool had already lost the stage to Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché), turning back and throwing her hand in the air at Guarischi for her actions in the sprint. Kool didn't mince her words when she spoke after the stage.

"I'm just really bummed that as a team we're sacrificing everything to let it come down to a sprint; you just want a fair chance," said Kool to Dutch publication .

"I think that fair chance has been taken away from me now. I find that very unsportsmanlike and very unfortunate.

"I haven't seen it back yet, but in my view, I was deliberately and intentionally pushed into the barriers. It wasn't just a little bit of a deviation from the line; it went from right to left. So yes, I find that very unsportsmanlike.

"Everyone knows images from the past. That goes through your head. I really want to win, but not much. And I also know that she won't give up easily, because she didn't do that to begin with."

The official results initially showed no consequences for Guarischi's sprint, but a post on AG Insurance Soudal's social media pages later on Wednesday evening confirmed that the Italian had been relegated, putting her at the back of the bunch in 85th.

"Nicola Steigenga has been promoted to third place in the final race classification of the first stage, following a race incident and the subsequent disqualification of the rider initially classified in third place," read a post from AG Insurance Soudal.

While the results page on the Eneco Tour's website has, at the time of writing, not been updated with the relegation for Guarischi, it is likely she was deemed to have broken rule 2.3.036 of the UCI regulations: "Riders shall be strictly forbidden to deviate from the lane they selected when launching into the sprint and, in so doing, obstructing or endangering others."

items.title: Taylor Phinney's return from retirement in UCI Track World Championships fizzles as US men miss finals in team pursuit
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
The highly-anticipated return of 2010 pursuit world champion Taylor Phinney to international competition at the UCI Track World Championships as the starter for Team USA's men's team pursuit squad ended on day 1, the quartet missing the medal finals. It's a step backward for the team, who finished fourth in last year's championships in Santiago, Chile.

Phinney made a late decision to join the USA Cycling programme, announcing his return in April, more than six years after he quit professional cycling at age 29 in 2019. His aim was to make the team for the Los Angeles Olympic Games to emulate his parents Davis Phinney and Connie Carpenter-Phinney, who both earned medals at the last Olympics there in 1984.

"The track was where I first found love and success in this sport, it was even the first discipline to break my heart when my specialty event, the individual pursuit, was removed from the Olympic programme, which prompted me to swiftly abandon the track and go all in on the road," Phinney wrote in April.

"Recently, the USA boys have been making huge strides in the Team Pursuit, and I couldn't be more stoked to be joining them in the chase for the Olympic Dream."

Phinney joined Ashlin Barry, Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson for the Team Pursuit on Wednesday, stepping in for last year's team member Graeme Frislie, who will compete in the Omnium, Madison and Scratch Race.

Speaking to the UCI on Wednesday before racing started in the Shanghai Velodrome on Chongming Island, Phinney said being back at the highest level on the track "feels like coming home in a lot of ways".

"It's really fun to ride with the guys," he said. "The technology has changed quite a lot, especially in team pursuiting.

"The positions have changed a lot. If you look at my position in the individual pursuit from 2009 - it was like completely wide open, and now everything is super close. So I think the position is more extreme, but the power numbers, they are not like so much different.

"I'm also racing as the starter, so I take a lot of the first minute of the race, getting everybody up to speed. I mean, we have a really strong team. It's kind of a question mark coming into the race, trying to understand where the other teams are at."

Phinney was realistic about the team's chances, saying before the race: "If we could do a top five, I think we would be really happy with that. And if we go into the finals, then we are more than stoked. But we'll take it one every one round at a time."

While the team did enough in the qualifying round to move on to the next heat, which determined the teams for the medal finals, they were unable to advance, setting times two seconds slower than the team did in 2025 and missing the medal round by half a second.

items.title: 'We have been in touch with the rider directly and apologised' – ITA responds to Valentina Cavallar's post about doping control on day her mother died
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The International Testing Agency (ITA) have apologised to Austrian rider Valentina Cavallar after an anti-doping officer arrived to test her following the death of her mother, while at the same time defending their procedures.

A doping control officer arrived at Cavallar's home "just a few hours" after her mother's death in September, she wrote, and the test was carried out with her mother in the next room.

"It was a moment that made me reflect on how easily we can forget that behind every athlete, there is a human being with a life, a family and emotions that do not simply disappear when the responsibilities of professional sport begin," added the SD Worx-Protime racer.

The ITA stated that Cavallar informed the doping control officer of her mother's death shortly after their arrival, but noted that she raised "no concerns or requests to postpone or discontinue the control" at the time.

"The International Testing Agency (ITA) extends its sincere condolences to Valentina Cavallar and her family following the loss of her mother," the statement to read.

"Since learning about the circumstances of the sample collection which took place on 5 September 2026 on Valentina Cavallar, the ITA looked into the context of the test.

"Neither the ITA nor the Doping Control Officer (DCO) were aware of the rider’s personal situation prior to arriving at her home. The DCO was informed of her mother’s passing upon arrival. According to the information gathered by the ITA since the rider’s Instagram post [Monday], Ms Cavallar and her family cooperated fully with the procedure, and no concerns or requests to postpone or discontinue the control were raised at the time or afterwards."

Under cycling's whereabouts system, riders must submit their location during a 60-minute period each day when they will be available for testing. Cavallar's situation occurred was a result of tragic coincidence, which the ITA acknowledged as an "exceptionally sensitive situation."

The doping control officer "endeavoured to pursue the procedure as discreetly, respectfully and swiftly as possible" with Cavallar and her family's support, the ITA's statement continued, before the organisation noted that it had reached out to her to apologise directly for the situation and any distress caused.

"We fully recognise that undergoing a doping control in these circumstances has added to her distress experienced at an extraordinarily painful time. We have been in touch with the rider directly and apologised.

"The ITA remains committed to ensuring that the protection of clean sport goes hand in hand with respect, compassion and care for athletes.

"We will also continue to always encourage athletes to report any concerns either during or after a doping control, so the ITA can take the appropriate measures to ensure a proportionate balance between the fight against doping and every athlete’s right to privacy and wellbeing."

items.title: Car enters course during Dutch race just four days after rider safety protest at Il Lombardia
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
A driver entered Wednesday's race route with around 70km to go just ahead of the breakaway, going in the same direction. Fortunately an in-race marshal was able to direct the green car to the side of the road from a motorbike, where it pulled over, allowing the three breakaway riders to pass safely.

Thankfully, the peloton were 1:44 behind, so by the time they reached the spot where the car was, it had already been diverted off the course. But it's the latest in a run of incidents which forced the riders' hands before the last Monument of the season.

Remco Evenepoel led the protest and delayed start in Italy on Saturday, giving a speech in which he said: "We want to make this statement because there's too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race. Unfortunately we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us, so we want to make this statement to show to the world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying in what we like the most to do."

Since his death, non-race vehicles have entered the route at the Giro dell'Emilia and Coppa Bernocchi, with a police motorbike going the wrong way during Tre Valli Varesine also knocking two of Tom Pidcock's Pinarello Q36.5 teammates out of the race.

Racing continued on Wednesday with Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) taking the win on the impacted Eneco Tour stage, but it's the latest in a run of shocking incidents just this year which forced the riders to take a stand at Il Lombardia.

At the same time as Evenepoel spoke, a scheduled shared statement was released by many of the riders in the professional peloton, in which they called for action from cycling's governing body, the UCI, and race organisers.

"As riders, we stand united against the unnecessary risk our lives are being subjected to," it read.

"[Last] week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses. Two riders crashed when they hit a motorbike who was driving the wrong way on the race route. Luckily both escaped with cuts and bruises, it could have been so much worse.

"This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer. Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the UCI and race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met.

"We are calling for the UCI and race organisers to take accountability and act. That means a serious, open conversation between riders, race organisers and the UCI resulting in concrete changes to how race routes are secured and managed.

"After five minutes, we raced as normal. We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one. We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones."

items.title: Giro del Veneto: Alessandro Covi pulls off first win of 2026 with well-timed sprint
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
An exceptionally long uphill drive for the line netted Jayco-AlUla racer Alessandro Covi a small bunch sprint victory on home soil in the Giro del Veneto on Wednesday.

Covi began his move some 300 metres to go on Vicenza's Monte Berico, and the Italian climber narrowly fended off a almost equally persistent Uno-X Mobility's Anthon Charmig to claim his first victory since a stage of the Vuelta a Asturias last year.

UAE Team Emirates-XRG had dominated proceedings in a tightly controlled bunch in the last 50 kilometres, first with Pavel Sivakov and then with World Champion Brandon McNulty. But their designated contender, France's Benoit Cosnefrôy, could not repeat teammate Isaac del Toro's win in Veneto last year and finally had to settle for third.

Covi's home triumph also ended a lengthy drought on victories for Jayco-AlUla, whose last win was a stage of 2026 Tour de France with Mauro Schmid.

Asked by race TV about his lengthy wait for a victory this year with Jayco-AlUla, Covi explained that it was impossible to predict when success would happen.

"You never know, it's difficult to win, but if it happens in October it's still a big victory," he said.

"Also, it's a nice race, I already did it a few times. It's the end of the season, a lot of the guys are tired - me too.

"But it's nice to win with a new jersey, [it's been] ten months before this victory arrived but it's a really nice victory."

In a race which took a long time to come alive, an early attack by eight low-profile riders, all of them from Continental or Club level bar one, Tommaso Nencini (Solution Tech Nippo Rali), was the standout feature of the first 100 kilometres.

Together with Nencini, the strongest in the all-Italian break - Francisco Carollo and his Swatt Club teammate, Giacomo Garavaglia , Kevin Pezzo Rosola and Thomas Rossetti (both General Store - Essegibi - F.Lli Curia), Leonardo Volpato (Campana Imballaggi - Morbiato - Trentino) and Riccardo Lorello (S.C. Padovani Polo Cherry Bank) had a two-minute lead on the pack as they passed the finish line for the first time in Vicenza, positioned two thirds of the way up the kilometre-long Monte Berico.

Having enjoyed their time in the warm autumn sunshine, with three local laps of five and 44 kilometres to go the last of the early breakaways was caught, in large part thanks to Pavel Sivakov's aggressive patrolling on the front of the bunch. Whilst a subsequent brief dig by Andrea Petrobon (Polti-VisitMalta) kept viewers entertained, there was little sense, though, that the main contenders were ready - or perhaps even able, given UAE's iron grip on proceedings - to make a long-distance move.

Once Petrobon was sucked in on the second-to-last ascent of the Monte Berico, the same grinding-down process continued, as UAE both controlled their most dangerous rivals with a high pace that simultaneously saw numerous riders shed out the back.

Pounding up the Arcugnano, the other, far gentler, main ascent on the circuit, Sivakov kept up the hard work whilst the white jersey of teammate and World Champion Brandon McNulty was never far away, either.

Tudor and Uno-X Mobility were the keenest to lead into the last full ascent of the Berico, but their efforts to break UAE's long stranglehold on affairs proved limited. Rather, Sivakov delivered one final effort, and as the bunch romped through the finish line and over the top of the grinding, steady climb, McNulty himself tried to go clear.

The American's flick-of-the-elbow gesture to co-attacker Christian Scaroni (XDS-Astana) to come through failed to spark enough of a reaction, though for his plan to work out, and instead there was a general regrouping. Marc Hirschi (Tudor) then rolled back the years with a searing uphill move, and while McNulty visibly sat up, both Hirschi and Fabio Christen (Pinarello-Q36.5) were able to go clear.

The two had a gap of almost ten seconds as they blasted along the undulating Arcugnano and McNulty then delivered yet another counter-attack to try and bridge across. However, the American could not make it alone, his rainbow jersey meaning he was heavily marked.

Even so, with six kilometres to go McNulty's constant accelerations did bring the bunch up to the two Swiss riders, and the American then almost single handedly ensured things remained together en route to the final, partial ascent of the Berico.

The front group of some 60 or 70 riders was still loosely together on the foot of the climb, as McNulty continued to drive away, only dropping back with 400 metres to go. However, Covi then launched a very long, sustained acceleration that saw the Italian both draw out the main group and stay ahead. Then whilst Charmig pushed Covi hard and Cosnefrôy and Christen were closing in fast, the 28-year-old Italian still had both the energy and resistance to manage to keep his rivals behind his front wheel all the way to the line.

"[Teammate Andrea] Vendrame was the guy we had for the sprint, but in the middle of the circuit, he came to me, said he didn't feel good and I should wait for the sprint," Covi explained afterwards about how he'd taken a much-needed victory for himself and the team.

"So I did exactly what he said, I never moved, I was always in the first group and I just tried for the sprint, and then I won. So that was super nice of Andrea, too."

items.title: Eneco Tour: Tim Merlier wins stage 1 sprint in Ede ahead of Dylan Groenewegen
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) sailed to victory on stage 1 at Eneco Tour launching a long-range sprint on the final 400 metres which had no reply from rivals.

Dylan Groenewegen (Unibet Rose Rockets) trailed in second while Gerben Thijssen (Alpecin-Premier Tech) took third ahead of Visma-Lease a Bike's Christophe Laporte.

The win moved Merlier 27 positions in the GC standings, now fifth overall. The top four positions held firm with just a two-second gap established from the opening prologue, Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) in the leader's jersey. Wessel Mouris (Unibet Rose Rockets) remains in second place, Laporte in third and Merlier's teammate Ethan Hayter in fourth.

Once at the flamme rouge, Soudal-QuickStep went into formation for Merlier on the right side of the course. At the final 90-degree corner with 400 metres to go, Nils Eekhoff from Picnic PostNL took the lead with riders from Unibet Rose Rockets, Visma-Lease a Bike and Alpecin just behind. Merlier exploded past them all and won by several bike lengths.

"It was quite hectic [in the final kilometre], and then we speed up, a really high speed. It was also difficult to find each other, but in the end we did really well," Merlier said about scoring his 13th victory on Wednesday.

"They bring me to a good position, and then I choose what I'm gonna do in the last 500 metres. I think it was a bit of a risk to go a bit further, but in the end, I can go in the slipstream, and speed up from behind the other guys. This kind of finish suits me really well."

After the 3.1km prologue to set the leaderboard, stage 1 took place with a flat 40-kilometre circuit on the north side of Ede tackled three times for 120km.

The peloton began the opening kilometres sizing up each other under the sunny skies, with the seven WorldTour teams massing at the front. Then a trio from a Dutch Continental squads were allowed to accelerate away - Johan Dorussen (Metec-SOLARWATT p/b Mantel), Rick Ottema (EEW-VDK Cyclingteam) and Luke Verburg (Azerion-Villa Valkenburg). .

Once on the second circuit, the three riders took shares in maintaining their breakaway and built a gap of 3:00. On the approach to Ede for the final loop, the gap began to fade as the peloton sensed time to position their fast men.

The breakaway trio scooped up all the bonuses at the intermediate sprint with 24km to go, but the peloton was only 15 seconds back with 15km to go. A wall of sprint teams, led by Soudal-QuickStep, Picnic PostNL and Unibet Rose Rockets, spread across the road and charged from behind to end the breakaway with 11km to go.

As the shadows began to stretch across the road with the sun beginning to fade in late afternoon, the peloton seemed to settle down on the next four kilometres heading back into the city limits. Visma-Lease a Bike edged to the front to support Christophe Laporte alongside Soudal-QuickStep while Unibet Rose Rockets held position on an outside line for Wessel Mouris with Lotto-Intermarché sending riders up. Lidl-Trek was there for race leader Jakob Söderqvist, biding their time as the finish neared.

It wasn't until 2km to go that the wide procession began to fracture, Soudal-QuickStep amping up the action. This straight run led to a defining sharp left-hand corner onto Arnhemseweg for the final 400 metres.

On that final corner, Merlier used the slipstream of his teammate Bert Van Lerberghe to vault from sixth position to first as he flew down the straightaway for the victory.

items.title: Track World Championships: Lorena Wiebes triumphs again in scratch race, Taylor Phinney returns with USA team pursuit squad
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
As was the case last year, rainbow jerseys were awarded for the women's scratch race and both the men's and women's team sprints, while qualification rounds for the men's and women's team pursuits came earlier in the day.

Lorena Wiebes scored the first gold of the Championships in the women's scratch race, while the Netherlands won the men's team sprint for the third year in succession and the home nation triumphed in the women's team sprint.

Read on for full reports and results from all of Wednesday's action.

Dutch star Lorena Wiebes took home the first rainbow jersey of the week, but only just, as she prevailed for the third year in a row at the scratch race. At the line, Wiebes edged out Lara Gillespie by centimetres to hang on and win as the Irishwoman launched from behind to take silver.

The 40-lap race saw a host of riders sweep to the front and up the pace as Wiebes' rivals sought to throw her off her stride ahead of the final. She lay in wait further back, comfortable in her position as she waited for the closing sprint.

After 10 minutes of racing, the riders reached the final 10 laps, with no big move at the front. With seven laps to go, France's Valentine Fortin leapt first as Wiebes jumped from the group to chase.

A regrouping followed as Wiebes dropped back again, and Belgium's Hélène Hesters led it into the final four laps. Wiebes came back, though, coming around the outside to hit the front again with two laps to go.

Gillespie was on her wheel, taking Portugal's Maria Martins with her as the lead trio opened up a gap on the rest on the final lap. Wiebes led around the final bend, but faded in the final metres before the line. Gillespie closed in but just missed out on passing the Dutchwoman, while Martins finished just behind the pair to take bronze.

"I think it's quite crazy. Of course you always go for the win, but it's always harder and harder to repeat it. Today was also really close. Lara came really close, but it was enough to win, and that's all I need," Wiebes said after her triumph.

"I think at the end, I needed to start my sprint a bit too early, but you also need to adapt to that situation, and I tried as good as possible. Lara was also really fast today, but I'm happy it was enough. That's the thing with scratch racing; it's also about positioning and tactics, not only the speed in the legs."
